chunks: Sense resistor pros and cons. The question: What are its pros and cons?
A sense resistor is simple, cheap, tiny and very linear: its voltage is exactly proportional to the current. It works from DC up to high frequencies and it shrugs off overloads.

Its drawbacks are side effects: it wastes power and drops voltage in the supply path, its small signal is easily swamped by amplifier offset, its resistance drifts with heat, and a fast current edge makes its tiny inductance add a false spike.
It also gives no electrical isolation.
Think of a speed bump on a road. It is cheap, it always works and it responds to every car the same way.
But every car has to slow down, which wastes energy, and a very busy highway would turn into a traffic jam. And the bump itself warms up and changes its behavior.
At a fixed sense voltage, loss grows linearly with current.
100 millivolts at 100 amps is 10 watts, which is why designers lower the sense voltage and rely on a low-offset amplifier at high current.
Insertion loss: the voltage and power the sensor takes from the circuit. TCR: how much the resistance changes with temperature, in parts per million per °C.
ESL: the tiny series inductance every real resistor has, a few nanohenries. Offset floor: the smallest current you can tell from zero, V os over R s .
Kelvin sensing: taking the sense voltage at the resistor's own pads.
A 5 milliohms shunt at 30 amps wastes 30 squared times 0. 005 equals 4. 5 watts, so it does not scale to high current.
Now the small-signal side: a 100 µV amplifier offset on a 10 milliohms shunt is 0. 0001 over 0. 01 equals 10 milliamps, so you cannot trust readings near that value.
Finally, a fast edge: with 5 nanohenries of inductance and a 10 amps step in 100 nanoseconds, the extra spike is 5 nanohenries times 10 amps over 100 nanoseconds equals 0.
5 volts, five times the 0. 1 volts real signal from 10 amps in 10 milliohms. That is the whole idea.
"Sense resistors are cheap, small, linear and accurate, they work from DC to high frequency, and they handle overloads.

The downsides are that they dissipate I to the 2R and drop voltage so they don't scale to very high current, their tiny signal means amplifier offset limits low-current accuracy, resistance drifts with temperature, parasitic inductance corrupts fast edges, and there's no isolation.
They also need Kelvin routing and a CSA that handles the common-mode voltage on the high side."
